# review

```go
import "github.com/shdeen/saferm/internal/review"
```

Package review decides which delete and move requests need approval, by testing the items that a request affects against the configured review patterns.

### Pattern rules

A pattern describes an item by its name or by its path. Patterns are compared with an item's real path, in which the symbolic links of the directories that lead to the item are resolved.

Two kinds of pattern:

- A path pattern starts with / or \~/, is exactly \~, or has a / before its last character. On Windows, a pattern that starts with a drive, such as C:/, is also a path pattern. A path pattern is compared with an item's full path.
- Every other pattern is a name pattern. It is compared with an item's own name, so it matches an item of that name in any directory. A / at the very end does not make a pattern a path pattern.

The directory that a path pattern is measured from:

- A pattern that starts with / describes a path from the root of the filesystem. / alone names the root directory.
- A pattern that is \~, or that starts with \~/, describes a path from the home directory. \~ alone names the home directory.
- Any other path pattern also describes a path from the root: build/output means /build/output.
- On Windows, a pattern that starts with a drive describes a path from the root of that drive and applies only to that drive. Every other pattern that is measured from the root uses the root of the drive or network share that holds the tested item.

Pattern text:

- \* matches any run of characters within one name, including none, and ? matches exactly one character. Neither matches /. A dot is an ordinary character to both.
- A set matches exactly one character: \[abc\] one of the listed characters, \[a\-z\] one character in the range, and \[\!abc\] or \[^abc\] one character that is not listed. In a path pattern, that character can be a / when the set covers it.
- \{a,b\} matches a or b, and each alternative may hold wildcards.
- In a path pattern, \*\* as a whole name stands for zero or more directories: /a/\*\* matches /a and everything inside it. Anywhere else, \*\* acts like \*.
- / separates directories on every system. On macOS and Linux, \\ makes the next character literal, so \\\* matches a \*. On Windows, \\ separates directories. A set that lists one character, such as \[\*\], matches exactly that character on every system. Every other character matches itself.

A character means the same thing wherever it stands in a pattern. Every name that holds a \*, ?, \[, \{, or \\ is compared by the matching library exactly as written.

A pattern that ends in / matches directories only. A symbolic link that points to a directory counts as one, and so does a link whose target cannot be inspected. A pattern that matches a directory protects everything inside it: an item is protected when a pattern matches the item itself or a directory above it.

The fixed part of a path pattern is the directory that the pattern is measured from, followed by the leading names up to the first name that holds a \*, ?, \[, \{, or \\. The fixed part is a location on disk:

- The symbolic links in its directories are resolved, so a pattern that is written through a link protects the real location. A fixed part that cannot be resolved is used as written.
- Its names hold no character with a meaning in patterns, so each one names the same directory as plain text and as pattern text.
- A pattern in which no name holds one of those characters spells out one item. When that item is a symbolic link, the pattern protects the link and the item that the link points to. Any other pattern that matches a link protects the link alone.

Letter case matters for a name exactly when the directory that holds the name treats two letter cases of it as two names. For a name pattern, the directory of the item decides. The names of a fixed part are compared one at a time, each by its own directory. The rest of a path pattern is compared in one piece, and the directory of the deepest name that has letters decides for the whole piece.

An empty pattern is ignored. A pattern is malformed when its text, without a trailing /, holds a set or alternatives that are not closed, a set that lists no character, a \} with no opening \{, or on macOS and Linux a \\ at its end. A malformed pattern protects every item.

### Requests

A request affects its source, every directory above the source, and, when the source is a directory, every item inside it. It needs approval when a pattern protects any of them.

## Constants

<a name="patternCharacters"></a>patternCharacters are the characters that give a name a meaning as pattern text: the wildcards, the start of a set, the start of alternatives, and the backslash.

```go
const patternCharacters = `*?[{\`
```

<a name="standInName"></a>standInName is a plain name that stands in for a directory when the library is asked whether a pattern matches the directory itself.

```go
const standInName = "directory"
```

<a name="Malformed"></a>
## func Malformed

```go
func Malformed(pattern string) bool
```

Malformed reports whether the pattern is malformed, as the package's pattern rules define it. An empty pattern is not malformed.

<a name="Match"></a>
## func Match

```go
func Match(patterns []string, source string, isDirectory bool, home string) (pattern string, unreadableDirectories []string)
```

Match returns the pattern that makes a delete or move of the source need approval, or an empty pattern when the request needs none. The patterns follow the package's pattern rules.

- source: the absolute path of the request's source, with the symbolic links of its parent directories resolved
- isDirectory: whether the source is a directory itself, not a link to one
- home: the home directory, whose symbolic links Match resolves

Match reports one pattern, chosen by list order:

- the first pattern in the list that protects the source;
- when none protects the source and the source is a directory, the first pattern in the list that protects an item inside it.

Match reads inside the source only when no pattern protects the source, and only directories that some pattern could protect an item inside. A name pattern always could. A path pattern could only when its fixed part is that directory, is inside it, or is above it. Match does not follow the symbolic links inside the source: it judges each link as an item under its own name and path.

When no item that Match can see is protected and it could not read a directory, it returns the first pattern in the list that could protect an item inside an unreadable directory, together with every unreadable directory. In every other case, unreadableDirectories is nil. With no patterns, Match reads nothing.

<a name="Validate"></a>
## func Validate

```go
func Validate(patterns []string) error
```

Validate returns ErrRuleMalformed, with a message that names the pattern, for the first malformed pattern in the list. It returns nil when the list holds none.

<a name="refoldName"></a>
## func refoldName

```go
func refoldName(itemName string) string
```

refoldName returns the name with each character replaced by the next character that Unicode counts as the same letter in another case, such as the capital ẞ for the small ß. A character with no such partner stays as it is.

<a name="resolveLinks"></a>
## func resolveLinks

```go
func resolveLinks(path string) string
```

resolveLinks returns the path with its symbolic links resolved, or the path as given when it cannot be resolved.

<a name="respellName"></a>
## func respellName

```go
func respellName(itemName string) string
```

respellName returns the name with each letter in its other letter case, when changing the case back gives the same letter. Every other character stays as it is. That includes a letter such as the dotless ı, whose capital is the capital of another letter: a directory that ignores letter case can still tell those two letters apart.

<a name="splitPath"></a>
## func splitPath

```go
func splitPath(path string) (volume string, pathNames []string)
```

splitPath splits a path into its Windows drive or share, which is empty on other systems, and the names that follow it.

<a name="location"></a>
## type location

location is one place where a path pattern applies: a directory, and the remaining pattern text, which is compared with the path below that directory.

```go
type location struct {
    // volume is the Windows drive or share that holds the directory, or empty.
    volume string
    // directory holds the plain names of the directory, from the root of the
    // volume down.
    directory []string
    // remainingPattern is the pattern text for the path below the directory.
    // Empty text matches the directory itself.
    remainingPattern string
    // fixedPart holds the plain names of the path that the pattern cannot match
    // outside of: the directory, followed by the final name when the pattern
    // spells out one item.
    fixedPart []string
}
```

<a name="locatePattern"></a>
### func locatePattern

```go
func locatePattern(startDirectory, patternText string) []location
```

locatePattern returns the places where a path pattern applies, given the directory that the pattern is measured from and the pattern text that follows that directory.

The leading names are the names before the first name that holds a pattern character. They are plain names, and the symbolic links among them are resolved. The text from that first name to the end is kept exactly as written, so every pattern character reaches the matching library.

A pattern in which no name holds a pattern character spells out one item. Its leading names are all the names but the last. When the item is a symbolic link, the pattern also applies to the item that the link points to.

<a name="newLocation"></a>
### func newLocation

```go
func newLocation(directory, remainingPattern string) location
```

newLocation returns the location of a directory given as a path.

<a name="parsePatternText"></a>
### func parsePatternText

```go
func parsePatternText(patternText, home, volume string) (nameText string, locations []location)
```

parsePatternText decides the kind of a pattern from its text, which has no trailing slash. For a name pattern it returns the text. For a path pattern it returns the places where the pattern applies, measured from the home directory, from the pattern's own Windows drive, or from the root of the volume.

<a name="requestMatcher"></a>
## type requestMatcher

requestMatcher tests the items of one request against the review rules.

```go
type requestMatcher struct {
    // rules are the prepared patterns, in list order.
    rules []rule
    // volume is the Windows drive or share that holds every tested item, or
    // empty.
    volume string
    // ignoresCase records, for each directory checked so far, whether the
    // directory treats two letter cases of one name as the same item.
    ignoresCase map[string]bool
    // source is the path of the request's source.
    source string
    // protectingRule is the index of the first rule found to protect an item of
    // the request, or the number of rules when none has been found.
    protectingRule int
    // unreadableDirectories lists the directories inside the source that could
    // not be read.
    unreadableDirectories []string
}
```

<a name="requestMatcher.appliesInside"></a>
### func \(\*requestMatcher\) appliesInside

```go
func (matcher *requestMatcher) appliesInside(testedRule *rule, directoryNames []string) bool
```

appliesInside reports whether the rule could protect an item inside the directory with the names. A name pattern always could. A path pattern could only when its fixed part is that directory, is inside it, or is above it.

<a name="requestMatcher.findRule"></a>
### func \(\*requestMatcher\) findRule

```go
func (matcher *requestMatcher) findRule(pathNames []string, ruleLimit int) int
```

findRule returns the index of the first rule before the limit that matches the item with the names, or the limit when none does.

<a name="requestMatcher.ignoresLetterCase"></a>
### func \(\*requestMatcher\) ignoresLetterCase

```go
func (matcher *requestMatcher) ignoresLetterCase(parentNames []string, itemName string) bool
```

ignoresLetterCase reports whether the directory with the parent names treats the item name and the same name in another letter case as one item. It asks the filesystem about each directory until one name settles the answer.

The spelling from respellName settles it either way. The name in capitals, the name in small letters, and the spelling from refoldName can only show that the directory ignores letter case, since a letter such as the dotless ı has a capital that belongs to another letter. Letter case matters when the name has no letters or names no existing item.

<a name="requestMatcher.isSameName"></a>
### func \(\*requestMatcher\) isSameName

```go
func (matcher *requestMatcher) isSameName(parentNames []string, itemName, patternName string) bool
```

isSameName reports whether an item's name and a plain name from a pattern are the same name in the directory with the parent names.

<a name="requestMatcher.itemPath"></a>
### func \(\*requestMatcher\) itemPath

```go
func (matcher *requestMatcher) itemPath(pathNames []string) string
```

itemPath returns the path of the item with the names on the matcher's volume.

<a name="requestMatcher.matchText"></a>
### func \(\*requestMatcher\) matchText

```go
func (matcher *requestMatcher) matchText(patternText, pathText string, parentNames []string, itemName string) bool
```

matchText reports whether the pattern text matches the whole of the path text. When the directory with the parent names ignores letter case for the item name, both texts are compared in small letters. An empty item name means that letter case matters.

<a name="requestMatcher.matchesLocation"></a>
### func \(\*requestMatcher\) matchesLocation

```go
func (matcher *requestMatcher) matchesLocation(ruleLocation *location, pathNames []string) bool
```

matchesLocation reports whether the item with the names lies at or under the location's directory and the path below that directory matches the rest of the pattern. The directory's names are compared one at a time. The directory itself matches only a remaining pattern that can stand for no name at all, as \*\* can.

<a name="requestMatcher.matchesRule"></a>
### func \(\*requestMatcher\) matchesRule

```go
func (matcher *requestMatcher) matchesRule(testedRule *rule, pathNames []string) bool
```

matchesRule reports whether the rule matches the item with the names. A malformed rule matches every item. A rule that ends in a slash matches only a directory or a symbolic link that points to one. It also matches a link whose target cannot be inspected, because that target may be a directory. A target that does not exist is no directory.

<a name="requestMatcher.readsDirectory"></a>
### func \(\*requestMatcher\) readsDirectory

```go
func (matcher *requestMatcher) readsDirectory(directoryNames []string) bool
```

readsDirectory reports whether a rule listed before the first protecting rule could protect an item inside the directory with the names.

<a name="requestMatcher.visitItem"></a>
### func \(\*requestMatcher\) visitItem

```go
func (matcher *requestMatcher) visitItem(itemPath string, directoryEntry fs.DirEntry, err error) error
```

visitItem tests one item inside the source directory against the rules that could still change the result: the ones listed before the first rule found to protect an item. It does not enter a directory that none of those rules could apply inside, and it records a directory that cannot be read. The walk ends once the first rule of the list protects an item.

<a name="rule"></a>
## type rule

rule is one review pattern, prepared for matching.

```go
type rule struct {
    // pattern is the pattern as configured, which a pending action records.
    pattern string
    // malformed reports whether the pattern is malformed. A malformed rule
    // matches every item, and its other fields are unset.
    malformed bool
    // directoriesOnly reports whether the pattern ends in a slash.
    directoriesOnly bool
    // nameText is the text of a name pattern, which is compared with an item's
    // own name. It is empty for a path pattern.
    nameText string
    // locations are the places where a path pattern applies. A name pattern has
    // none.
    locations []location
}
```

<a name="parseRules"></a>
### func parseRules

```go
func parseRules(patterns []string, home, volume string) []rule
```

parseRules prepares the patterns for matching items on the volume, in list order. It leaves out empty patterns.
